title: Targeted microstructural authoring through additive manufacturing of metals
abstract:
Abstract Metal three-dimensional printing—also known as additive manufacturing (AM)—provides a unique opportunity for materials engineers to locally tailor the microstructure of engineering alloys over a range of length scales. Although multiple metal AM processes exist, the market is dominated by laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) systems. Properly applied, L-PBF has the potential to allow localized “authoring” of the metallurgical architecture in a number of ways, including the careful manipulation of key processing parameters or using advanced beam shaping technologies to locally control cooling rate through important phase-transformation temperatures. These strategies are, in effect, locally changing the thermal history of the material being fabricated. From a metallurgical perspective, these strategies fall within the well-established processing–structure–properties paradigm, despite their reliance on modern, highly specialized equipment. In this article, we examine how some of these emerging strategies are being used to locally tailor the microstructure in AM alloys and reflect on how this presents opportunities to “dial-in” site-specific mechanical properties in high-performance engineering parts. columnar to equiaxed transition (CET)), (2) allotropic phase transformations

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Additive manufacturing (AM) provides an opportunity to “author” the microstructure and thus the properties of engineering components through the judicious control and manipulation of processing parameters in real time. This is the processing–tructure–properties paradigm of materials science/metallurgy and is governed by physics. Localized control of microstructure is not new; it has been used in many other technologies, including, but not limited to, shot/shock peening, machining, the production of dual-microstructure turbine disks through advanced forging and heat-treatment schedules, surface carburization, traditional fusion welding technologies and solid-state welding processes such as rotary friction welding.

A multitude of metal AM technologies exist, such as blown powder directed energy deposition, wire-arc deposition, material extrusion, sheet lamination, and laser powder bed fusion, and a comprehensive overview of these metal AM methods has been provided by Armstrong. 1  Although multiple metal AM processes are available, the market is dominated by laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) systems and, properly applied, L-PBF has the potential to allow localized “authoring” of the microstructure.

The creation of bespoke microstructures using L-PBF can be achieved in multiple ways. Examples include: (1) Varying the laser processing parameters such as the hatch spacing, beam power, and beam velocity. 2 , 3  (2) Employing local rescanning strategies to achieve ( in situ ) site-specific heat treatments. 4  (3) Employing laser-beam shaping methods to locally control the cooling rate. 5 , 6  In effect, all of the methods listed above are site-specifically changing the thermal history of the material either by highly targeted post-solidification heat treatments or varying the cooling rate/thermal gradient during the solidification process. For example, changes in cooling rate through a phase-transformation temperature have a pronounced effect on the microstructural unit size, such as the ɑ-lath width and colony size in ɑ + β titanium alloys 7  or the secondary dendrite arm spacing (SDAS, λ 2 ) in stainless steels. 8  Faster cooling rates will lead to mean values of λ 2  that are orders of magnitude smaller than those associated with the slowest cooling rates. It is such changes to the effective slip length of dislocations that controls the mechanical properties; the more barriers there are to dislocation movement, the harder the material becomes. So, while from a production perspective these could appear to be different strategies, from a materials science viewpoint they often lead to similar, but distinct, physical processes on the mesoscale.

Other methods of microstructural engineering in AM include: (4) Local chemistry control, which is well appropriated to directed energy deposition (DED) technologies, affecting not only alloy composition, but also microstructure. 9 , 10  (5) Hybrid methods, where AM and sintering have been combined to yield composite microstructures. 11 , 12  (6) Doping of powders, for example, with oxide dispersion strengtheners (ODS) to improve high-temperature creep performance. 13  (7) L-PBF of dissimilar metal materials. 14  (8) The deliberate seeding of volumetric defects such as lack-of-fusion voids to quantify their effect on fatigue performance following hot isostatic pressing and heat treatment. 15

This article focuses on the direct methods to locally engineer the microstructure in L-PBF materials (methods 1—3). Initially, the key process variables in L-PBF technologies will be defined in the following section (L-PBF process variables). Subsequent examination of these methods, through the lens of the metallurgical mechanisms that facilitate such site-specific microstructural control, will be explained in the subsequent sections. These are (a) “ Solidification conditions ” (i.e., the columnar to equiaxed transition [CET]), (b) “ Allotropic phase transformations ,” and (c) “ Recrystallization .” We include a discussion of the current state of the art, as well as some suggestions about potential future opportunities.

sections.heading: L-PBF process variables
paragraphs: L-PBF is a near-net-shape production technology that uses a focused laser beam to selectively melt or fuse together metallic powder. The feedstock powder, of a given particle-size distribution (PSD), is supplied from one or more hoppers and applied across a baseplate using a raking or rolling mechanism. 16 ,  17 – 18  A laser beam is subsequently rastered over selected areas of a given layer powder to fabricate a two-dimensional “slice” of the desired part. The baseplate is moved down by a desired height and the process is repeated multiple times until fabrication of the entire part is completed. This enables engineers to rapidly produce a three-dimensional part directly from a computer-aided design (CAD) model, thus reducing the need for multiple materials processing steps.

Many processing variables for L-PBF exist and a considerable number of studies have investigated how these process variables can affect build quality. 19 ,  20 ,  21 ,  22 ,  23 – 24  On commencing a given build process, the majority of processing variables are not typically considered to change and have, therefore, been designated as “fixed variables.” These include, but are not limited to, the powder bed temperature, chamber inert gas type and flow rate, laser-beam type (e.g., Nd:YAG), powder feedstock type, and powder size, shape, and chemistry. Conversely, some processing parameters are more commonly changed during the build process; these are the radius of the laser beam (r B ), which can be controlled by the focal offset distance (FOD), the laser-beam shape, the power of the laser beam ( q ), the rate at which the laser beam traverses the powder bed, that is, the velocity ( v ), the spacing between the individual laser raster lines, that is, the hatch spacing ( h ), and distance that the build plate moves down between individual layers, that is, the layer height ( l ). Some examples of typical ranges used for these processing parameters can be found in Table I in Reference 16. For this review, it is these processing parameters that are perceived to be the key process variables for the purposes of site-specific microstructural engineering.

For a fixed layer height and hatch spacing, a decreased laser-beam power coupled with a higher beam velocity results in lower values for the volumetric energy density. The volumetric energy density can be increased by either increasing the beam power, slowing down the laser beam or by the selection of smaller values for hatch spacing and layer height. During a build, modulating the energy density will change the local thermal history of the material being processed. This could be due to variation in the solidification rate ( R ), thermal gradient ( G ) or the degree of subsequent remelting (or reheating) due to the overlap between adjacent melt pools and heat-affected zones. This, in turn, will affect the evolution of microstructure as the material cools through its freezing range and any subsequent solid-state phase-transformation temperatures.

Equation  1 , however, cannot take into account the temperature of the powder bed, the beam radius, beam shape, or the thermophysical properties of the material being fabricated. Furthermore, nominally the same values for  E  can also result in different melt pool sizes, morphologies, and resulting microstructures. 25  Therefore, caution should be taken when comparing values for  E  across different alloy systems or L-PBF platforms. Nevertheless, it is a useful comparator for identifying potential changes in thermal history within a build 2 , 3  or between different samples of the same material fabricated on the same L-PBF platform. 17  Alternative metrics, which take into account factors such as the beam radius and material thermophysical properties, have also been developed. These metrics allow comparisons between different L-PBF platforms and alloys. They include dimensionless enthalpy 26 , 27  and normalized energy density. 16

Two further key process variables are also important for site-specific microstructure control: The laser-beam size and laser-beam shape. For a fixed beam power and velocity, changing the beam radius will modify (1) the power density (W/m 2 ) and (2) the duration for which the material is exposed to the laser beam (i.e., the interaction time). Both of these will influence whether heat transfer is by conduction only, or whether vaporization takes place due to the highly concentrated heat input. 29  In the field of welding, these two modes are known as “conduction mode” and “keyhole mode,” and will also affect the melt pool geometry and thermal history of the material being processed by L-PBF. 30  A similar effect can be achieved by changing the FOD of the laser beam: For example, Tang et al . 31  investigated how offsetting the focal plane affected the thermodynamic behavior of the melt pool and the resulting microstructure in L-PBF Ti-6Al-4 V.

More recently, researchers have also been experimenting with the shape of the laser beam and how this influences the microstructure in L-PBF parts. 5 , 32  Typically, the power density of a laser beam follows a Gaussian distribution, with a peak power density peaking in the center of the beam that decreases with increasing distance from the beam center point. Using a fiber laser module that allowed switching of the beam profile between Gaussian and ring-shaped profiles, Grünewald et al. 32  elegantly showed how crystallographic texture and grain size could be controlled within a single specimen of 316L stainless steel.

sections.heading: Solidification conditions
paragraphs: Local control of the solidification conditions is arguably the longest established method of microstructural authoring in AM. Work by Gaumann et al. 33  highlighted that it was possible to predict and control the solidification microstructure by understanding how the manufacturing strategy affected the thermal conditions within the melt pool. This early work, which predates the first ASTM standardization of AM terminology 34  by nearly a decade, was done using a process they called epitaxial laser metal forming, which now falls into the directed energy deposition (DED) category rather than L-PBF. Despite the difference in technology, the controls they used (laser power, velocity, and part preheat) can be readily transferred to L-PBF.

Most published work available today (e.g., References  35 ,  36 – 37 ) was conducted to promote equiaxed grain structures, rather than the columnar structure that is typical in L-PBF. In contrast, the objective of Gaumann et al .  was unusual in developing process settings that would promote epitaxial growth of a single large grain on a single-crystal turbine blade repair. They demonstrated that a modification of Hunt’s model 38  (proposed in 1984), allowed the observed microstructure to be mapped against solidification conditions in the melt pool. These solidification conditions are: The temperature gradient ( G ) and solidification rate ( R ). The product of  G  and  R  is the cooling rate; with higher cooling rates ( GR ) generally leading to similar, but finer, microstructures during solidification. An idealized version of such a solidification map is shown in  Figure   2 . Figure 2 Schematic example of a solidification map indicating predicted microstructures associated with different values of  G  and  R . Inspired by several sources. 39 ,  40 – 41  CET, columnar to equiaxed transition.

Of particular interest were the conditions where the microstructure underwent a columnar to equiaxed transition (CET). 33  This occurred when constitutional supercooling was sufficient to nucleate enough equiaxed grains ahead of the columnar dendritic front. The volume fraction of equiaxed grains would be a function of the temperature gradient ( G ) and solidification rate ( R ) within the melt pool, as well as factors unique to each material, such as the number of nucleation sites available.

Combining this theory with numerical modeling to calculate  G  and  R , allowed Gaumann et al. to identify a range of laser processing parameters that resulted in the desired microstructure. Since then, a similar methodology has been used by numerous authors (e.g., References  35 ,  36 – 37 ) to either explain the microstructure observed and/or identify manufacturing parameters that achieve a given microstructure. Many attempts have been made to adapt L-PBF melt strategies toward the equiaxed condition, but fully equiaxed grains have not yet been routinely achieved. Some authors suggested that the key to achieving equiaxed grains lay in new alloys designed to promote CET 36 , 42  while others changed the thermal conditions by the introduction of new melting strategies, often using multiple beams. 40 , 43 , 44

Even within a single melt pool, however, the situation is complex, with conditions varying both spatially and temporally. 35 , 37 , 40 , 45  Models often suggest that, as solidification progresses, conditions move toward the CET at the center of the weld.  Figure   3  is a composite figure illustrating the change in calculated conditions (Figure  3 a), a schematic of the resulting microstructure (Figure  3 b) and microstructure measured using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) (Figure  3 c). Figure 3 Predicted solidification conditions and resultant microstructure in a single melt track. Adapted from: (a) Reference  46 ; (b) Reference  40 ; and (c) Reference  47 . CC-BY-4.0.

Despite these complexities, there have been successful demonstrations of developing melt strategies to move away from columnar and to equiaxed grains. 4 , 44 , 48 , 49  Moreover, by local modification of the solidification conditions, functionally graded parts have been generated.

An early example was provided by the flexibility of electron beam melting (EBM), where the beam can be moved so fast as to behave as several discrete beams. Careful planning of the melt process was used to manufacture Inconel parts with variable microstructure. 44 , 49  Furthermore, this work showed that the strong texture associated with epitaxial columnar growth can be reduced by the nucleation of equiaxed grains in areas with nonstandard melt processes. Thus, a method to control the texture has been demonstrated.

The strong texture often associated with EBM components is a function of both the inherent characteristics of the material, as well as the typical melt strategy applied. 45  Cubic alloys have a preferred ❬100❭ growth direction, and grains where this direction best aligns with solidification tend to outcompete less favorably oriented grains. By systematic variation of the hatch direction it is possible to control the texture. 48 Figure   4  shows EBSD data collected from a sample where several (50) layers were melted with identical hatching orientation, before rotating. As a result of the similar solidification conditions, bands of distinct texture were formed and detectable by EBSD. Figure 4 Electron backscatter diffraction data illustrating the possibility to alter the texture of a stainless-steel alloy by changing hatch direction in a systematic fashion. IPF, inverse pole figure; LEGO, layer-wise engineering of grain orientation; BD, build direction. Reprinted from Reference  48 . CC-BY-NC-ND.

sections.heading: Allotropic phase transformations
paragraphs: Engineering materials such as steels, titanium alloys, and zirconium alloys undergo solid-to-solid phase transitions at certain temperatures well below their melting ranges. Such solid-state transitions are referred to as allotropic phase transformations. Understanding how the addition of alloying elements alters these particular temperatures has been a key area of exploration in metallurgy for well over 100 years. In addition to the chemical composition of the alloy, the rate at which the material is heated or cooled through these phase-transformation temperatures controls the resulting microstructure and thus the mechanical properties, which are of vital importance to engineers. Varying the heating and cooling rates through these allotropic phase-transformation temperatures is, consequently, an important strategy in controlling microstructure during thermomechanical processing 50 , 51  and welding of engineering alloys. At high cooling rates (i.e., under nonequilibrium conditions), insufficient time is available for diffusional transformation to occur and the transition between phases is accommodated by the large-scale, nondiffusional movement of atoms to form a hard, but brittle martensitic or martensite-like structures. 51 ,  52 – 53  Due to their poor ductility, alloys containing a large volume fraction of martensite or martensite-like microstructures are generally unsuited to structural applications and post-quenching tempering treatments may be required to achieve a balance between strength and ductility.

The high cooling rates associated with L-PBF technologies (10 3 –10 6  K/s) tend to provide favorable conditions for martensitic or martensite-like microstructures to form. 54 , 55  This is especially the case when the powder bed temperature is well below that of the martensitic start temperature ( M S ). Considerable attention has therefore been given to understanding the phases present in materials processed via L-PBF 56 − 58  and, where a martensitic or martensite-like microstructure is present (or expected to exist), how to tailor the processing parameters to control its volume fraction without the need for postbuild tempering. 17 , 59

Early efforts to control martensite content include the work of Xu et al., 17  who were able to tune the L-PBF processing parameters to promote the formation of a fine (ɑ + β) lamellar microstructure during fabrication of the titanium alloy Ti-6Al-4 V. Similar to steels, martensite in titanium alloys is associated with poor ductility and there are clear benefits to controlling the volume fraction of martensite during the L-PBF process. This was achieved by varying the volumetric energy density ( E ) and the focal offset distance (FOD) of the laser beam. Low FOD and higher  E ’s favor a fine, lamellar microstructure with a lath width in the range 0.2–0.3 µm. It was proposed that the (ɑ + β) lamellar microstructure did not form directly upon cooling through the β-transus, but instead via the  in situ  decomposition of martensite, which occurred as a result of the repeated heating and cooling cycles as multiple layers were fused together. Although this work did not explore whether martensite volume fractions could be locally engineered, it did demonstrate that, by controlling thermal history, the mechanical properties could be readily tailored without the need for any post-L-PBF heat treatment.

By leveraging the allotropic phase transformation that takes place in Ti-6Al-4 V, the work of Chen and Qiu 59  extended the earlier approaches of Xu et al. 17  to produce a banded microstructure, alternating between layers of martensite and a fine (ɑ + β) lamellar structure ( Figure   5 ). This was achieved by re-rastering a lower power laser beam over selected layers of the build, which led to the local decomposition of martensite during the build process. The mean height of these bands (in the  z -direction) was in the range of 55–75 µm (Figure  5 a–b), with the band height depending upon the power of the laser beam used during the reheating process (Figure  5 b). The authors reported that such a banded microstructure led to a modest decrease in yield strength (~200 MPa) compared with the baseline, non-rescanned specimen, but almost doubled the elongation to failure from 5% to approximately 10 percent. Although limited to microstructural manipulation on a layer-wise basis, this approach clearly demonstrated the potential for L-PBF to be used to control the volume fraction of constituent phases on a length scale appropriate for the site-specific tailoring of microstructures. Figure 5 (a, b) Etched microstructures of Ti-6Al-4 V showing a range of banded microstructures in laser powder bed fusion Ti-6Al-4 V, which alternate between layers of martensite and a fine lamellar structure of ɑ and β phases. The effect of reheating laser-beam power on the mean width of the microstructural bands is shown in (c). Adapted from Reference  59 . CC-BY-4.0.

More recently, Esmaeilzadeh et al. 5  employed an advanced beam shaping module to tailor the laser-beam power density (W/m 2 ) during L-PBF of Ti-6Al-4 V. Both thermal camera monitoring and finite element modeling (FEM) confirmed a significant reduction in the cooling rate for the tailored beam compared with the standard laser beam profile. Thermal camera data showing the temperature profile for a tailored beam and standard Gaussian beam are shown in  Figure   6 a–b. The authors concluded that the reduction in cooling rate associated with the tailored beam suppressed martensite formation and resulted in a fine (ɑ + β) lamellar microstructure. Switching between beam shapes therefore enabled three-dimensional, site-specific control of the cooling rate through the  M S  temperature and thus the ability to fine-tune the microstructure on a length scale close to that of the molten pool. This was demonstrated by using a two-stage process to inscribe the letters “EPFL” into a Ti-6Al-4 V specimen (Figure  6 c–d); (1) printing using a tailored beam shape; and (2) remelting targeted regions to spell “EPFL” using a Gaussian laser-beam profile. This had the effect of introducing martensite or (martensite-like structures) into a matrix of fine (ɑ + β) lamellae, which was formed during the initial tailored beam stage. Figure 6 (a) Thermal camera data showing a “tailored” beam and (b) a more typical Gaussian laser-beam profile. (c) A confocal microscopy image of the letters “EPFL” inscribed into a Ti-6Al-4 V laser powder bed fusion specimen by leveraging laser-beam shaping. A scanning electron micrograph of the region delineated by the yellow box in (c), which shows the interface between the martensitic microstructure (ɑ′) and the fine (ɑ + β) lamellae matrix is given in (d). Adapted from Reference  5 . CC-BY-4.0.

Moving away from titanium alloys, Fields et al. 2  were able to spatially control the hardness of a precipitation hardened stainless steel (17–4 PH) by varying the volume of fraction of ferrite and martensite ( Figure   7 ). This was achieved by spatial modulation of the volumetric energy density ( E ) during the L-PBF process. To locally modulate  E , the authors kept power, hatch spacing, and layer height constant, but altered the beam velocity in predefined volumes of the build: High beam velocities, corresponding to low values of  E , led to a martensitic microstructure with hardness values around 500 on the Vickers scale (H V ). On the other hand, a dual-phase microstructure of ferrite and martensite was formed in zones where higher energy densities were implemented, with hardness values closer to 450 H V . To explain this observation, the authors proposed that martensite always forms first on cooling, irrespective of the value of  E  used during the printing process. The dual-phase microstructure of ferrite and martensite forms during reheating of the region between adjacent scan lines, and only in the lower  E  condition. Nevertheless, this mixture of ferrite and martensite is reportedly thermally stable and remains unchanged by postbuild heat treatments. Figure 7 Light micrograph (a) and microhardness map (b) showing the letters “UCI” inscribed into a 17-4PH stainless-steel specimen fabricated via careful tuning of laser powder bed fusion processing parameters. The higher hardness regions in (b) (delineated by the letters by “UCI”) correspond to a martensitic microstructure, while the surrounding matrix is composed of a dual-phase microstructure of martensite and ferrite. Adapted from Reference  2 . CC-BY-4.0.

sections.heading: Recrystallization
paragraphs: Recrystallization is a process where a new grain structure forms in a heavily deformed metal or alloy. 60  Recrystallization can be brought about by either (1) plastically deforming a metal or alloy at low homologous temperatures and subjecting it to a post-deformation annealing treatment i.e. static recrystallization; or (2) through continuous plastic deformation at relatively high homologous temperatures i.e. dynamic recrystallization. Industrial processes such as forging and rolling will generally lead to a recrystallized microstructure through the whole section thickness of the workpiece. On the other hand, if sufficient plastic deformation can be introduced locally, via surface deformation processes such as shot peening 61  or laser shock peening, 62  then targeted recrystallization can be achieved upon subsequent annealing. 63 , 64

In the case of a peened single-crystal nickel alloy, Holtham et al. 63  showed that increased dislocation density in the volume of material immediately below the peened surface caused localized recrystallization to take place during a 100-h heat- treatment temperature at 1100℃. Although these experiments did not concern a part produced via L-PBF, their work is an instructive example of how targeted recrystallization may be achieved. This is illustrated in  Figure   8 a–b. Here, the degree of plastic strain induced by the peening process is inferred from EBSD mapping via plots of the kernel average misorientation (KAM) 65  (Figure  8 a). Upon annealing, the highly deformed region immediately below the shot peened surface recrystallized to form randomly orientated (and largely strain-free) grains with a mean diameter of 55 µm (Figure  8 b). Figure 8 (a) Cross-section kernel average misorientation (KAM) map of a shot peened, single-crystal Ni-alloy prior to heat treatment. (b) A KAM map of the same alloy following heat treatment at 1100℃, which shows recrystallization to have taken place leading to largely strain-free grains. (a, b) Adapted from Reference  63 . © 2026 Springer Nature. (c– e) KAM maps of 316L stainless steel fabricated by laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF). Adapted from Reference  3 . CC-BY-4.0. The effect of hatch spacing on the crystal misorientation distribution in as-built material is given in (c, d). An example of microstructural authoring, achieved via the tuning of L-PBF processing parameters to yield site-specific recrystallization is given in (e). BD refers to the build direction and SD the scanning direction.

A similar result was achieved by Kalentics et al. who combined L-PBF with laser shock peening to induce targeted recrystallization in 316L stainless steel. 64  Due to strain hardening, the authors reported that laser shock peening caused the subsurface hardness to increase from approximately 290 H V  in the as-built condition to values in the range of 320–380 H V  for the L-PBF and laser shock peened samples. Following annealing, the plastically deformed subsurface region recrystallized, again leading to an equiaxed grain structure similar to that shown in Figure  8 b–c. This study provides an example of how recrystallization can be leveraged for targeted microstructural control in L-PBF parts. This approach is limited in that it can only be achieved on surfaces that are accessible to peening processes.

To overcome the limitations of peening, attempts have recently been made to directly trigger recrystallization through the careful selection of AM processing parameters. 3 , 66  Unlike thermomechanical processes such as rolling or forging, control of dislocation density in AM parts cannot only be achieved via mechanical deformation. 66  The density of dislocations can instead be controlled by modifying the L-PBF processing parameters to induce more (or less) thermal cycles in a given volume of material. 66 ,  67 – 68  Such repeated thermal cycling during L-PBF is akin to a low-cycle thermal fatigue process, where small amounts of plastic strain are introduced by successive heating and cooling cycles.

In the approach used by Gao et al., 3  two L-PBF processing parameter combinations were employed to locally control the grain size, shape, and crystallographic texture of 316L stainless-steel specimens. These were chosen for their anticipated effect on the thermal stability of the microstructure during postbuild annealing: (1) A high thermal stability parameter set, which used a larger hatch spacing (low E) with no laser rescanning. (2) A low thermal stability parameter set, where a smaller hatch spacing (higher E) was employed along with localized rescanning of the laser beam to selectively remelt the previously consolidated material. Figure  8 c–d shows KAM maps of the high and low hatch spacing conditions, respectively. The low hatch spacing condition ( h  = 10 µm) led to a greater crystal misorientation distribution within the area analyzed, which can be inferred as a higher density of dislocations, while the opposite was the case for the high hatch spacing condition ( h  = 35 µm). By comparing Figure  8 a, d, parallels can be drawn between the dislocation structure associated with the low hatch spacing condition (Figure  8 d) and that introduced into the near-surface regions by the shot peening process (Figure  8 a). In both cases, the regions associated with a high dislocation density have KAM distributions shifted toward higher values on the crystal misorientation scale.

Upon annealing, specimens fabricated using the larger hatch spacing ( h  = 35 µm) did not recrystallize (i.e., they were thermally stable). Initial investigations showed however, that specimens fabricated with a hatch spacing of  h  = 10 µm only partially recrystallized. To explain this observation, the authors performed energy-disperse spectroscopy (EDS) measurements and proposed that recrystallization was restricted by the microsegregation of solute alloying elements (Cr, Mo) at solidification cell boundaries. To overcome this chemical heterogeneity, and therefore promote full recrystallization, localized remelting using the laser beam was performed to homogenize the material. This reheating of the material was sufficient to promote diffusion (and therefore reduced chemical heterogeneity) in the heat-affected zones adjacent to the melt pools, but insufficient to initiate recrystallization. Provided that targeted remelting was applied beforehand, the high dislocation density associated with the low hatch spacing condition led to full recrystallization in selected volumes of the deposited material during annealing (blue zones in Figure  8 e). The recrystallized region, denoting the acronym “AM” in binary code, were composed of randomly orientated, equiaxed grains of an average size of 20 µm. This is in contrast to the high thermal stability processing parameter set (high  E ), which did not recrystallize during the postbuild annealing and the resulting microstructure was typical for AM materials i.e. large (~120 µm) columnar grains with a strong crystallographic texture.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: The previously discussed approaches to site-specific microstructural design fall broadly into two categories: Direct local microstructure control during fabrication, resulting in architectured microstructures negating any postbuild annealing or heat treatment. Examples include the adaptation of melt strategies to promote equiaxed grain formation or controlling the volume fraction of phases such as martensite. Changes in microstructure that only appear after subsequent annealing or heat-treatment stage. This may be achieved through the spatial modulation of dislocation density of dislocations by the careful selection of processing parameters. This approach is analogous to the use of “invisible ink,” where a hidden message is only revealed after the application of a substance or ultraviolet light.

The thermal stability of a bespoke microstructure is an important consideration if any postbuild operations are required. For example, to minimize any internal porosity, L-PBF components could be hot isostatically pressed following fabrication. 15 , 69  In the case of microstructures comprising a mixture of martensite and more thermodynamically stable phases, such a post-processing step will likely lead to the disappearance of any microstructural gradient as metastable martensite decomposes to a more thermodynamically favorable state. Therefore, and depending on application, there are advantages to using a two-stage process to achieve site-specific microstructure control.

As a result of a recent series of advances in AM technologies, opportunities now exist to explore targeted microstructure control in high-performance engineering components, that is, to “dial-in” site-specific microstructures (and therefore mechanical properties) in regions where specific material performance requirements are required. By leveraging local recrystallization for example, fine equiaxed microstructures can be introduced in highly stressed (e.g., load bearing regions) of complex engineering components. Finer microstructures are not only likely to increase material strength, but also hinder the nucleation of fatigue cracks in parts subjected to fluctuating loads in service. For engineering components with less complex geometries this has already been achieved in powder metallurgy “dual microstructure” turbine disks. These critical rotating components balance a resistance to fatigue crack initiation against cold-dwell crack propagation performance, have been produced by using site-specific heat treatments (see Gabb et al. 70 ). The manufacture of targeted microstructure control in L-PBF parts has been demonstrated at an academic level. Whether this is achievable in geometrically complex engineering parts, is an important next step to maximize the potential that this technology can bring.

This article has reviewed some of the approaches used to create bespoke microstructures in L-PBF specimens. These have been discussed through the lens of the metallurgical mechanisms that control the microstructural evolution of engineering alloys, including phase transformations and recrystallization. These are well-established concepts in the field of materials science. It is clear that applying the metallurgical insights gained from other metal processing methods, such as casting, thermomechanical processing, and surface treatments, are able to unlock the potential for microstructural authoring in AM alloys.
